source: Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF), General Directorate of Agriculture, Department of Agricultural Extension — 'បច្ចេកទេសដាំដំណាំឪឡឹក' (Watermelon Cultivation Techniques), 2017.
text:
Downy mildew is a fungal disease of watermelon. Symptoms appear as yellow-brown angular spots on the leaves, usually starting on the older, lower leaves of the plant; under high humidity these spots can spread quickly to cover most of the leaf. The disease develops and spreads fastest during humid, rainy periods, when dew or moisture stays on the leaves for extended periods, and is more severe once the plant canopy becomes dense (typically around the flowering and fruit-development stage).

Prevention: choose disease-tolerant/resistant varieties where available; avoid planting too densely so that air can circulate through the canopy and leaves dry more quickly; promptly remove and destroy infected leaves found in the field; avoid overhead watering that wets the foliage, and water in the early part of the day so leaves dry before nightfall; ensure the field drains well and does not hold standing water; and avoid repeatedly planting watermelon or related cucurbits on the same land season after season. Preventive fungicide sprays using active ingredients such as Metalaxyl, Prochloraz, or Fosetyl-Al can be applied before symptoms appear, particularly during the rainy season or periods of high humidity.

Treatment once infected: cut off and destroy infected leaves, removing them from the field rather than leaving them on the ground; spray with fungicides such as Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, Propamocarb, or Trifloxystrobin, rotating between different active ingredients to reduce the risk of the fungus developing resistance, and following label rates and pre-harvest intervals.
